UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Constitution Pipeline Company, LLC                                             Docket Nos. CP13-499-006
Iroquois Gas Transmission System, L.P.                                                     CP13-502-003

                       ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT COMMENTS

        Catskill Mountainkeeper; Clean Air Council; Delaware-Otsego Audubon Society;
Delaware Riverkeeper Network; Maya K. van Rossum, the Delaware Riverkeeper; Food &
Water Watch; Riverkeeper, Inc.; Sierra Club; and Waterkeeper Alliance (“Intervenors”), joined
by Natural Resources Defense Council, hereby submit comments on the Environmental
Assessment (“EA”) 1 for Constitution Pipeline Company LLC’s (“Constitution”) Constitution
Pipeline Project and Iroquois Gas Transmission System, L.P.’s (“Iroquois Gas”) Wright
Interconnect Project (collectively the “Project”). Intervenors’ EA comments supplement their
April 7, 2014, comments 2 on the 2014 Draft Environmental Impact Statement, which are fully
incorporated by reference in these EA comments. As with the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission’s (“FERC” or “the Commission”) 2014 Final Environmental Impact Statement
(“FEIS”), the improperly conducted EA fails to adequately assess and mitigate impacts to air,
water, species, and natural resources, and fails to adequately consider cumulative impacts and
less harmful alternatives.

        We also note that the 30-day comment period is wholly inadequate for this matter, which
involves roughly 15 years of studies, an FEIS and the current EA, as well as project variations
and major changes in environmental conditions. Intervenors, supported by the State of New York
and other commenters, requested a 40-day extension of the comment period, which FERC has
thus far inexplicably declined to adjudicate. The difficulty in preparing meaningful and adequate
comments in that limited time frame was compounded by the comment period including the end
of summer when several attorneys and clients had prescheduled vacations, and then by
observance of Jewish high holidays. By failing to extend this plainly inadequate and truncated
comment period, FERC only weakens the EA and undermines its own consideration of the
Project.

    I.   Intervenors Continue to Object to FERC’s Consideration of the Petitions for
         Reissuance Instead of Requiring New Applications Under Section 7.

       Intervenors maintain, as explained in their previous filings in the above-captioned
dockets, 3 that the process FERC is undertaking to “reissue” a certificate of public convenience

reissuance. The Natural Gas Act grants FERC the authority to issue a certificate only in response
to a full application, 15 U.S.C. § 717f, and the Petitions Constitution and Iroquois Gas submitted
requesting reissuance fail to comply with all statutory and regulatory requirements for
applications. Furthermore, the certificate that Constitution and Iroquois Gas ask FERC to reissue
was vacated by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit and must be treated as a legal
nullity. FERC must, therefore, dismiss the Petitions and require new applications for certificates
to be filed. Because new applications for certificates are required, a new review of the Project
under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”), 42 U.S.C. § 4332, and new applications
for state water quality certifications under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA”), 33
U.S.C. § 1341, are required. FERC’s previous declaratory order finding that the State of New
York waived its CWA Section 401 authority as to the Constitution Project has been vacated by
the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit and therefore has no legal effect. Even if it
were not vacated, the declaratory order is irrelevant because a new application for a certificate
under the Natural Gas Act, which Constitution must be required to submit in order to revive its
pipeline Project, triggers a new CWA Section 401 process. In any event, FERC was incorrect
that New York waived its authority in 2015.

       By submitting comments on the EA, Intervenors do not waive the above objections to
FERC’s failure to dismiss the Petitions. The instant NEPA process is being wrongly conducted
under a docket that should have been closed years ago and pursuant to petitions for reissuance
that FERC was required to dismiss out of hand. In order to ensure preservation of all of their
arguments, Intervenors provide the following comments in response to FERC’s EA.

 II.    The Project’s Benefits Are Speculative and There Is No Demonstrated Need for the
        Project.

       While the question of market need for the Project is beyond the scope of what
Commission staff evaluate in a NEPA review and is ultimately determined in an order by the
Commission, Intervenors raise it here because of the way information developed during NEPA
review is used in weighing harms and benefits in FERC’s ultimate decisionmaking under the
NGA and because of how the market need for the Project informs the purpose need defined for
the NEPA review.

        FERC uses a multi-step process, starting with market need, to determine whether a
Project is “required by the present or future public convenience and necessity,” 15 U.S.C.
§ 717f(e), and thus can be granted a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. First,

 FERC determines whether the Project can move forward without subsidization by existing
customers, which requires a showing of market need. New Jersey Conservation Found. v. FERC,
111 F.4th 42, 50 (D.C. Cir. 2024). “Relevant factors for determining market need may include,
but are not limited to, ‘precedent agreements, demand projections, potential cost savings to
consumers, or a comparison of projected demand with the amount of capacity currently serving
the market.’” Id. (quoting Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities, 88
FERC ¶ 61,227, ¶ 61,747 (Sept. 15, 1999), clarified, 90 FERC ¶ 61,128 (Feb. 9, 2000), further
clarified, 92 FERC ¶ 61,094 (July 28, 2000)). “If FERC finds a market need, it moves on to the
second step, where it must determine whether adverse impacts are outweighed by public
benefits.” Id. If the public benefits outweigh the harms, then FERC moves on to complete an
environmental analysis and to weigh all harms, including environmental harms, against the
Project’s benefits. Id. at 51. See also Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line Company, LLC, Order
Issuing Certificate, 192 FERC ¶ 61,184, P 24 (Aug. 28, 2025) (describing multi-step process).

        The “goal” of NEPA review is “to inform agency decisionmaking,” Seven Cnty.
Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle Cnty., Colorado, 605 U.S. 168, 173 (2025); therefore, the goal of
FERC’s NEPA review is to inform its ultimate decision about whether “a project’s public
benefits (such as meeting unserved market demand) outweigh its adverse effects (such as
deleterious environmental impact on the surrounding community),” as is required to grant a
Certificate under Section 7 of the NGA. See City of Oberlin, Ohio v. FERC, 937 F.3d 599, 602
(D.C. Cir. 2019).

         FERC need not reach the step of weighing the Project’s full suite of harms, including
environmental harms, against its benefits, however, because there has been no showing of market
need on the docket. To date, nine months after filing its Petition for Reissuance, Constitution still
has no precedent agreements. As explained in Intervenors’ Protest, 5 precedent agreements are
considered the most important evidence of market need for a project, so the absence of any
precedent agreements for any of the Project’s capacity should be taken as important evidence of
the lack of market need. Without precedent agreements, the only evidence of the alleged market
need in the record are Constitution’s conclusory assertions of the Project’s predicted benefits in
its Petition for Reissuance and the S&P Global study (Attachment A to Constitution’s Petition)
that purports to support Constitution’s assertions but, as explained in Intervenors’ Protest, 6 does
not actually establish that the gas carried by the pipeline would have the downstream benefits
asserted. If there is, in fact, no market need for the Project and it would not create any public
benefits, then even minimal environmental harms would outweigh the Project’s non-existent
benefits, meaning FERC could not approve it.

       The purpose and need stated in the EA relates back to the question of market need. The
EA quotes Constitution in stating that the purpose of the Constitution Pipeline is to “increase
supply diversity and improve operational performance, system flexibility, and reliability in the
New York and New England market areas.” 7 The EA states that the purpose of the Wright
Interconnect Project “is to provide 650,000 dekatherms per day of leased firm transportation
capacity for natural gas from the terminus of the CPP in Wright, New York, to downstream

III.       FERC Must Prepare an EIS for the Project.

       FERC must prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (“EIS”), rather than an EA,
because the Project is likely to have reasonably foreseeable significant impacts and because
FERC’s regulations require preparation of an EIS for major pipeline projects that, like the
Constitution Pipeline, create new rights-of-way. In 2014, FERC recognized that the Constitution
Pipeline and Wright Interconnect Project would have foreseeable significant impacts that
required preparation of an EIS. Although there is no evidence indicating that the Project’s
impacts will be less significant more than a decade later, FERC prepared only an EA.

        NEPA requires all federal agencies to prepare an EIS examining the “reasonably
foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action” before taking any agency
action “significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(C); see
also 42 U.S.C. § 4336(b)(1). An agency may prepare an EA only if the proposed agency action
“does not have a reasonably foreseeable significant effect on the quality of the human
environment, or if the significance of such effect is unknown.” 42 U.S.C. § 4336(b)(2). The
impacts of constructing and operating the Project are likely to be significant and their
significance is not unknown or unknowable. Therefore, an EIS is required.

        In order to serve its purpose of adequately informing FERC’s substantive
decisionmaking, Seven Cnty., Colorado, 605 U.S. at 173, FERC’s NEPA review must take the
form of an EIS that fully evaluates the Project’s impacts, including the relative impacts of
alternatives, and analyzes potential mitigation measures that FERC may impose as conditions on
a Certificate. FERC must be fully informed about a Project’s environmental impacts in order to
determine that the Project’s benefits outweigh its harms as is required for FERC to grant a
Certificate. New Jersey Conservation Found., 111 F.4th at 62; City of Oberlin, 937 F.3d at 602.
FERC must also be fully informed about whether to exercise its “power to attach to the issuance
of the certificate and to the exercise of the rights granted thereunder such reasonable terms and
conditions as the public convenience and necessity may require,” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e), including,
as FERC’s regulations require, consideration of mitigation measures, including ones an applicant
did not propose, but which could be more effective than those proposed, 18 C.F.R. § 380.7.

       FERC’s regulations also state that an EIS will “normally” be prepared for “[m]ajor
pipeline construction projects under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act using rights-of-way in

IV.      FERC Has Not Corrected the Errors in the FEIS.

        FERC has claimed that the Commission “will ultimately determine in the Order whether
the prior and current NEPA analyses are sufficient to fulfill its NEPA obligations.” 11 As
Intervenors highlighted in their Scoping Comments, the FEIS contained serious errors that have
not been corrected. 12 FERC has continued to rely heavily on this flawed FEIS despite its reliance
on incomplete information, its flawed and inadequate analysis, and the changed factual and legal
landscape. In fact, FERC relied on the outdated and flawed FEIS analysis entirely for seven of
the fourteen resource areas considered and significantly in many other areas of analysis. 13 As
indicated by the Intervenors’ Scoping Comments, the FEIS inadequately analyzed the Project’s
impacts on water resources, wetlands, soils, wildlife, air quality, blasting activities, and mud pits,
as well as missing data and incomplete mitigation planning. 14 Furthermore, the FEIS failed to
properly evaluate reasonable alternatives, including a meaningful “no action” option, and several
environmental impacts were understated or excluded from public review. 15

         Intervenors incorporate the entirety of their Scoping Comment here. To the extent that the
EA continues to rely on the flawed underlying analysis of the FEIS, this analysis must be redone
to satisfy its NEPA obligations.

 V.      FERC Is Incorrect That There Have Been No Changes Since the FEIS for Certain
         Resources Not Carried Forward.

        Since issuance of the 2014 FEIS, conditions along the proposed Constitution Pipeline and
Wright Interconnect Projects have materially changed in several respects. Although the EA
acknowledges many of these changes, it repeatedly concludes that the FEIS remains valid and
that impacts would not substantially differ from those analyzed in the FEIS. In doing so, the EA
relies on generalized statements rather than undertaking a comprehensive reassessment of
environmental consequences and accordingly fails to adequately account for the effects of
changed environmental conditions, updated scientific information, altered land uses, and newly
identified sensitive resources.

VI.      FERC Must Adequately Consider Less Harmful Alternatives, Including
         Compressor Station Electrification.

        Both NEPA and the NGA require FERC to consider alternatives, including: the no-action
alternative of denying the application; granting only part of the application, such as approving a
smaller capacity project than proposed; or imposing conditions upon any certificate granted, such
as requiring compressor stations to be powered by electricity to minimize air pollution. 39

        The Natural Gas Act provides that, in response to an application under Section 7, the
Commission may issue a certificate “authorizing the whole or any part of the operation, sale,
service, construction, extension, or acquisition covered by the application, if it is found that . . .
the proposed [activity], to the extent authorized by the certificate, is or will be required by the
present or future public convenience and necessity.” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e). The Commission also
has “the power to attach to the issuance of the certificate and to the exercise of the rights granted
thereunder such reasonable terms and conditions as the public convenience and necessity may
require.” Id. Section 7 therefore imposes upon the Commission a requirement to consider what
conditions the public convenience and necessity may require and whether to, in the alternative,

        Because the “goal” of NEPA review is “to inform agency decisionmaking,” Seven Cnty.,

     A. Electric Compressors Alternative

        While FERC finds that using an electric compressor station, instead of gas turbine
powered compression, for the Wright Interconnect Project “would be technically feasible,” 40
FERC arbitrarily rejects that alternative without adequate consideration. FERC’s reasons for
rejecting that alternative are: (1) that based on information that Iroquois Gassubmitted, 41 “it
would not be economically practical and would not meet WIP’s objectives due to the increased
time” and (2) that FERC “cannot conclude that the alternative would provide a significant
environmental advantage due to the required powerline construction and in light of the current
proposal’s demonstrated compliance with the [National Ambient Air Quality Standards]
NAAQS.” 42 These reasons are unsupported in the record, and FERC has not provided
information about the relative benefits of electric and gas powered compressors in a way that
allows the public to meaningfully compare these alternatives.

        As to economic feasibility, Iroquois Gas did not provide any substantiation for its
estimates that installing an electric compressor station (and the additional 3-mile power line
required for it) would add 6 years of additional time to the project, $32 million in construction
costs, and $4.5 million in annual cost for electrical service. 43 Nor did FERC or Iroquois Gas
address whether some of those costs, the timeline, or the required footprint for any additional
transmission line could be reduced by using onsite renewable generation paired with batteries to
provide some of the electricity required.

        As to environmental advantages, FERC is incorrect to suggest that there would be no
environmental advantage to electrification merely because the Wright Interconnect Project, as
proposed with gas-powered compressor units, is modeled to comply with the NAAQS. As
explained further below, see infra Section VII, substantial health benefits can be achieved by
reducing pollution even further below the NAAQS because pollution, even at levels below the
NAAQS, causes health impacts such as asthma attacks or even premature death. While the D.C.
Circuit has recently affirmed FERC’s practice of using NAAQS compliance as a metric to

the primary contributing factor in the loss of interior forest.

        Fragmentation creates an increase in the amount of forest edge (the interface between
forest and non-forest). This transitional zone or “ecotone” is fundamentally different in structure
and functionality from an interior forest system. Edge habitat is characterized by increased light
levels on the forest floor, reduced soil moisture, and a high degree of biological invasion from
non-native invasive organisms. Dramatic changes can occur in the soil chemistry and the
associated micro biota. The top layer of the soil profile, the rich organic duff, begins to dry out
and the primary decomposition community begins to shift from fungal to bacterial. This
transition in the decomposition community has direct implications for a host of vertebrate and
invertebrate species that depend upon this rich organic humus for survival and reproduction. It
also directly affects the type and quality of tree regeneration in the ecotone. Typically extending
up to 300 feet into the forest, edge impacts are more than mere esoteric considerations of interest
to the scientific community, these changes have direct economic implications for both
landowners (including state and local governments) and society.

        In addition to the impacts to species and the natural environment, recent estimates have
placed the annual costs to the U.S. economy from the biological invasion of invasive species at
approximately $21 billion dollars. 157 Invasive organisms within terrestrial forest environments
tend to be early successional species that respond favorably to site disturbance. Disruption of
native plant cover and the exposure of the forest floor to sunlight provides an opportunity for
these organisms to establish satellite populations. These populations eventually radiate into the
adjacent forest, displacing native species and retarding desirable tree regeneration. 158 Dispersal
(vectoring) mechanisms and/or corridors are required for these non-native species to colonize
new locations and access roads, pipelines, and vehicular traffic associated with natural gas
infrastructure is ideally configured to serve this function.

        For years after decommissioning, the landscape legacy of forest edge from pipeline
corridors, access roads and other infrastructure will continue to disrupt ecosystem functioning as
non-native organisms repeatedly colonize exposed areas and impede desirable tree regeneration.
Invasive species suppression and the eventual restoration of these disturbed sites to forested
systems will require resources of a significant financial and temporal scale. While published
information is scarce, it is in the professional experience of restoration practitioners in this region
that the reasonable reconstruction of forest canopy and understory diversity can cost between
$5,700 and $14,200 per acre. The suppression of invasive plant species is also a major, recurring
155
    Id. at 5–6.
156
    Id. at 6.
157
    Id.
158
    Id. at 7.

                                                  28
 expense with the initial years’ treatment often incurring costs between $1,400 and $3,500 per
acre. Invasive treatment in subsequent years typically drops in cost by approximately 50% per
year over the first three years. The EA fails to adequately assess these costs and does not
propose that the Project sponsors bear or mitigate such economic impacts. The limited
compensatory mitigation proposed in the FEIS and EA contemplates funding third-party groups
to conduct mitigation activities, but such activities do not mitigate economic or other harms (i.e.
recreation and loss of uses) to impacted landowners.

        As the effects of forest fragmentation may not immediately manifest themselves
following the disturbance, monitoring is often suggested as a methodology to balance and
modify the level of fragmenting activity in accordance with the conservation of forest-related
ecosystem services. Unfortunately, these effects may not be linear in nature and thus are not
always amenable to an adaptive management approach. Biological systems may possess
thresholds that provide little indication of impending adverse impacts until sudden system
collapse. The EA fails to carry forward the vegetation resource for analysis. 159 Twelve years
have transpired since the FEIS, and it is unreasonable to assume that substantial changes have
not occurred in the vegetative communities located within the impact area of the Constitution
Pipeline. As an example - more than one fifth of the Project right of way (the Pennsylvania
section) was clearcut over a decade ago by Constitution contractors and then subsequently
abandoned without restoration or active management, this vegetative community has absolutely
undergone significant modification. FERC assumes that the cleared areas have begun to
regenerate and that invasive plant species “may have” colonized these areas. FERC also indicates
in the Environmental Information Request No. 2 (June 25th, 2026), that Constitution has
committed to updating the invasive species surveys following reinstatement of the Certificate
Order. This is circular reasoning as a determination that the vegetation has not undergone
“substantial changes” can only be made after a survey. The successional trajectory of the forest
systems that have been clearcut and then abandoned for over a decade will display a species
composition and habitat type radically different from the previous cover type. The introduction
and colonization of invasive species into a disturbed linear corridor of over 25 miles that lacks
active management will, in all probability, be significant. Wind, water, human and animal
vectoring will have distributed seed and plant propagules across this area. A newly cleared linear
corridor is extremely attractive to off-road vehicles–a frequent contributor to invasive plant
dispersal and continual site disruption.

        Given the clearcutting and the temporal lag between the FEIS and the EA, a new
vegetation analysis must be a component of the Environmental Assessment. Invasive Species
Management Plans FERC utilizes the state-specific Invasive Species Management Plans (ISMPs)
as a component of the rationale for not carrying forward vegetation in the EA analysis. As such,
it is important to highlight the major deficits in these plans. Given the high degree of
commonality between both the New York and Pennsylvania plans, the concerns detailed here are
applicable to both documents. The ISMPs stated goal is to goal is to “…control the invasive
species to the extent that wetlands and uplands are not dominated by the invasive species to the
point where the functions and values of the systems/habitats are adversely compromised.”
However, there are no measurable metrics indicated in the documents that would allow for
quantitative assessment of progress towards that goal. It is common practice in invasive control

159
      EA tbl. A.3-1.

                                                29
 contracts for the land management entity to require a certain percentage of invasive cover
reduction be achieved after a given time frame. This provides a clear benchmark whereby project
success can be measured. Constitution’s Plan lacks such a requirement.

        While the ISMPs acknowledge the difficulty in achieving eradication of invasive species
due to issues such as seed drift and/or colonization from off-site locations, they fail to mention
two critical vectoring mechanisms that are of extreme importance when dealing with right-of-
way construction and maintenance: (1) the latent seed bank residing in the soil (2) the chronic
encouragement of invasive colonization due to the expansion of edge habitat.

        Depending upon the species, invasive seeds and propagules can survive in the soil for
years. Japanese stiltgrass (Microstegium vimineum) and Autumn Olive (Elaeagnus umbellate)
have both been frequently found within the proposed Project right-of-way. These species have a
seed viability in the soil (the timeframe in which they can lay dormant) that exceeds five years.
This latent seed bank germination cannot be addressed within the brief three-year time frame in
which Constitution intends for treatment and monitoring. Constitution recognizes in the
Preliminary Migratory Bird and Upland Forest Plan that in the construction of the Project, a
significant amount of interior forest will be converted to edge forest. The nature of edge habitat –
disturbed areas of high light penetration, creates ideal conditions for biological invasion. One of
the primary transport mechanisms for invasive plants are birds that preferentially roost at the
forest edge and subsequently defecate invasive seeds into the understory. It is important to
recognize that, until such time that the forest canopy closes over the right-of-way, the edge
habitat that has been created will be highly susceptible to invasive colonization. Once
established, small populations can expand into off-right-of-way properties and disrupt forest
regeneration, soil chemistry, habitat, hydrology, and ultimately land value. Recognizing the
chronic nature of the biological invasion threat that is promoted by the creation and perpetuation
of edge habitat, it is obvious that the EA’s proposed treatment timeframe that only lasts for three
years is wholly inadequate. Invasive suppression needs to continue for the Project lifespan as the
perpetuation of edge habitat via the three-year mowing and suppression of tree canopy in the
ROW will create ideal conditions for repeated infestation. The ISMPs clearly state that
Constitution “will not” treat areas outside its proposed construction right-of-way for invasive
species. This is highly problematic given that the edge habitat created by the Constitution Project
will encourage biological invasion in the adjacent forest lands for the entire service life of the
right-of-way. Suppression costs will eventually fall upon the adjacent property owner should an
infestation become established.

        In sum, the EA for the Constitution Pipeline project is flawed as it fails to analyze
vegetation resources that have, in all probability, substantially changed in twelve years since the
Final Environmental Impact Statement was produced. In addition, the EA relies upon inadequate
ISMPs as part of the rationale for avoiding updating the vegetation analysis. Without an updated
invasive plant survey and vegetation analysis, mitigation and management strategies cannot be
effectively developed and implemented. Should the Certificate of Public Convenience and
Necessity be issued by FERC without a proper analysis, widespread disruption of forest
ecosystems and local watershed resources will occur. Restoration of these systems following the
eventual cessation of natural gas transmission will be a monumental cost incurred by both the
taxpaying public and adjacent private property owners.

                                                30
 XII.       FERC Must Adequately Consider Cumulative Impacts.

       FERC’s environmental review of the Project falls short of its obligation to assess
cumulative impacts. None of the recent legal developments in NEPA law, such as the Council on
Environmental Quality’s (“CEQ”) recission of its NEPA regulations, removes the obligation to
consider cumulative impacts. The EA is not even clear on whether it is carrying forward
cumulative impacts as a category to be assessed anew in 2026 versus relying solely on the FEIS.
To the extent that the EA gestures at cumulative impacts analysis, its analysis falls short of the
hard look required by NEPA. To the extent it relies on the FEIS, the FEIS’s analysis of
cumulative impacts was insufficient. 160

       A. FERC Has a Legal Obligation to Consider Cumulative Impacts.

        A proposed action’s consequences can only be understood in context. A cumulative
impact is an impact of the project under review—in particular, it is “the impact on the
environment which results from the incremental impact of the action when added to other past,
present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions regardless of what agency” reviews those
other actions. El Puente v. U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs, 100 F.4th 236, 249–50 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
(quoting 40 C.F.R. § 1508.7) (emphasis added). A cumulative-impacts analysis thus includes
consideration of the effects of the project at hand alongside the effects of other reasonably
foreseeable future projects whose effects will overlap with the same geographic area as the
proposed action’s effects. El Puente, 100 F.4th at 249; TOMAC, Taxpayers of Mich. Against
Casinos v. Norton, 433 F.3d 852, 864 (D.C. Cir. 2006). Without considering cumulative effects,
agencies may not realize that a proposed project would “represent the straw that breaks the back
of the environmental camel.” Grand Canyon Tr. v. FAA, 290 F.3d 339, 343 (D.C. Cir. 2002)
(quoting Hanly v. Kleindienst, 471 F.2d 823, 831 (2d Cir. 1972), and noting that Hanly preceded
the CEQ regulations implementing NEPA and interpreted NEPA itself).

        Withdrawal of CEQ regulations regarding NEPA did not eliminate the requirement to
consider cumulative effects. That is because cumulative effects, like other kinds of effects, are
just as much “reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action.” 42
U.S.C. § 4332(C)(i). Cases reviewing agency actions that preceded the CEQ regulations found
that NEPA itself imposes the obligation. Kleppe v. Sierra Club, 427 U.S. 390, 410 (1976)
(stating that when multiple proposals for related actions “that will have cumulative or synergistic
environmental impact upon a region are pending concurrently before an agency, their
environmental consequences must be considered together”); Balt. Gas & Elec. Co. v. NRDC, 462
U.S. 87, 106–07 (1983) (“NEPA requires an EIS to disclose the significant health,
socioeconomic and cumulative consequences of the environmental impact of a proposed
action.”).

       CEQ, for its part, agrees that NEPA itself requires consideration of cumulative effects.
CEQ’s post-withdrawal guidance encourages agencies to continue considering all “reasonably
foreseeable” effects, “regardless of whether or not those effects might be characterized as

160
      DEIS Comments at 21–24.

                                                31
 ‘cumulative.’” 161 In prior guidance, CEQ had emphasized that “cumulative effects analysis is
essential to effectively managing the consequences of human activities on the environment.” 162
Cumulative effects are not just an important part of the problem, but can be the most important
issue: “[e]vidence is increasing that the most devastating environmental effects may result not
from the direct effects of a particular action, but from the combination of individually minor
effects of multiple actions over time.” 163 Although CEQ’s interpretation of NEPA does not bind
FERC or the courts, CEQ’s expertise, developed over decades of administering NEPA, warrants
persuasive weight. See, e.g., Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 402 (2024)
(quoting Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms v. FLRA, 464 U.S. 89, 98, n.8 (1983)).

        Nor did Seven County eliminate the requirement to analyze cumulative effects. Seven
County concerned indirect effects—particularly, effects “separate in time or place from the . . .
project at hand.” Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle Cnty., 605 U.S. 168, 186 (2025).
Seven County did not discuss cumulative effects—effects that are impacts of the project under
review, “result[ing] from the incremental impact of the action when added to other past, present,
and reasonably foreseeable future actions regardless of what agency” reviews those other
actions, El Puente, 100 F.4th at 249 (quoting 40 C.F.R. § 1508.7) (emphasis added), rather than
occurring elsewhere in “time and place,” and which provide context needed to understand the
“single project within the authority of the agency,” Seven Cnty., 605 U.S. at 190.

        B. The EA Does Not Adequately Evaluate Cumulative Impacts.

        As an initial matter, the EA is not actually clear whether it is carrying forward cumulative
impacts review or is relying entirely on the FEIS’s cumulative impacts review. The “Summary of
Resources and Effects Analyzed,” 164 which specifies which resources were carried forward and
which were not, does not list Cumulative Impacts. The EA says that “[p]rojects that could affect
the environmental baseline are broadly similar to the types of other projects described in section
4.13.6 of the FEIS and include oil and gas development and transmission in Susquehanna
County, Pennsylvania, and electric generation and transmission, renewable energy,
transportation, and commercial and residential development in all five of the counties
encompassing the Project Area.” 165 This statement suggests that FERC is relying on the FEIS’s
assessment of cumulative impacts (contained in FEIS section 4.13.16), however a statement that
projects are “similar” is not sufficient to absolve FERC of its duty to evaluate the cumulative
impacts of this Project in combination with those identified projects to determine whether they
are significant. At the same time, however, FERC seems to indicate that it has identified new
projects with potential cumulative impacts and considered them: “Several reasonably foreseeable
planned activities were identified in the watersheds and/or counties in the Project Area that may
influence the environmental baseline in which the Projects would be constructed.” 166 The public

161

Environmental Policy Act at 5 (Feb. 19, 2025), https://nepa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/CEQ%20Memo-
Implementation%20of%20NEPA%2002.19.2025.pdf.
162
    CEQ, Considering Cumulative Effects Under the National Environmental Policy Act at 3 (Jan. 1997),
https://nepa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Considering%20Cumulative%20Effects%20Under%20NEPA_0.pdf.
163
    Id. at 1.
164
    EA at 4–7, tbl. A.3-1.
165
    Id. at 22.
166
    Id.

                                                   32
 is left to wonder what planned activities FERC assessed, their relation to the Project, and
whether they will impact environmental or other conditions.

       Without a clear understanding of what FERC has or has not evaluated, the public cannot
meaningfully assess and comment on FERC’s cumulative impacts analysis. Informing the public
and providing meaningful opportunity for public comments are key purposes of NEPA review.
Dep’t of Transp. v. Pub. Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 768 (2004) (stating that NEPA review is
designed to “provide a springboard for public comment” (citation modified)); Marsh v. Or. Nat.
Res. Council, 490 U.S. 360, 371 (1989). FERC’s lack of clarity undermines those key purposes.

        To the extent that the EA does make a half-hearted attempt at cumulative impacts review,
without using the word “cumulative,” that review falls far short of the required hard look. First,
FERC fails to actually identify the “reasonably foreseeable planned activities” it mentions in the
EA. The EA describes these activities at a very high level of generality, for example listing “20
transportation projects in Susquehanna, Broome, Delaware, and Schoharie Counties; and 4
industrial developments located in Delaware and Schoharie Counties, and 11 other projects.” 167
The EA refers readers to several filings Constitution made for the specifics of the projects. 168 It
again points to Constitution’s filings for the specifics of the “new developments, identified after
issuance of the FEIS . . . as overlapping or immediately adjacent to the CPP, including a quarry
near milepost (MP) 6.2 and an industrial facility near MP 120.” 169 This lack of specificity and
explanation within the EA itself undermines the public’s ability to understand FERC’s analysis
and meaningfully comment on it.

         Second, FERC’s evaluation of the cumulative impacts of these projects is superficial and
acknowledges only cumulative impacts during construction, while ignoring ongoing cumulative
impacts during the operational life of the Project. FERC acknowledges only that “[d]uring
construction, these projects would affect resources within the same subwatersheds and/or
counties as the Projects, including groundwater resources through excavations and potential
groundwater withdrawals, biological resources through vegetation clearing and habitat
disturbance, and surface water and wetland disturbances through crossings, import of fill, or
erosion events.” 170 FERC further notes that it “expect[s] these effects would be temporary and
localized.” 171 FERC does not explain how impacts from vegetation clearing and habitat
disturbance would be only temporary if projects, including the Project at issue here, permanently
alter the landscape. See supra Section IX.B. Nor does it justify treating water and wetland
impacts as only temporary when construction of projects often permanently alters the water flow
through streams and wetlands and tree clearing can lead to ongoing increased erosion throughout
the life of a project.

 DISCUSSION



A careful review and analysis of the EA and the associated materials submitted by

Constitution reveals several areas of concern with respect to the maintenance of the

ecological integrity of terrestrial ecosystems and the corresponding impacts upon aquatic

resources. The plans in the FEIS, to the extent supplemented by the EA, do not adequately

provide for protection and sustainable regeneration of forest systems along the

proposed pipeline route. The canopy cover provided by the forested lands through which

the proposed pipeline cuts is of extreme importance to both the quality and quantity

of water that flows within the regional drainages.



Background



Forests filter contaminants, moderate stream temperatures and buffer flow volumes

associated with precipitation events. They are the structural foundation upon which the

ecological integrity and health of this region’s biological resources are built. The link

between percent forest cover and water quality is clearly established in the scientific

literature. As an example, reductions in forest cover are directly correlated with negative

changes in water chemistry, such as increases in nitrogen, phosphorus, sodium, chlorides,

and sulfates, and with reductions in stream marcroinvertebrate diversity (Jackson and

Sweeny 2010).



Forest fragmentation because of anthropogenic landscape modification is well

recognized within biogeographic theory and conservation biology as a leading cause of

local species extinctions (extirpation). It can also cause dramatic shifts in the floral and

faunal composition of woodland communities. Sub-lethal impacts to floral and faunal

                                               5
 populations (population isolation, reduced genetic fitness and diversity) have also been

associated with disruptions to forest connectivity (Clark, et al. 2010). The USGS has

documented a disproportionate level of interior forest loss (two to three times greater than

overall forest loss) over the last several years from natural gas infrastructure construction

in areas such as Susquehanna County, PA (Slonecker 2013). Pipeline corridors have

proven to be the primary contributing factor in the loss of interior forest.



Fragmentation creates an increase in the amount of forest edge (the interface between

forest and non-forest). This transitional zone or “ecotone” is fundamentally different in

structure and functionality from an interior forest system. Edge habitat is characterized by

increased light levels on the forest floor, reduced soil moisture, and a high degree of

biological invasion from non-native invasive organisms. Dramatic changes can occur in the

soil chemistry and the associated micro biota. The top layer of the soil profile, the rich

organic duff, begins to dry out and the primary decomposition community begins to shift

from fungal to bacterial. This transition in the decomposition community has direct

implications for a host of vertebrate and invertebrate species that depend upon this rich

organic humus for survival and reproduction. It also directly affects the type and quality of

tree regeneration in the ecotone.



Typically extending up to 300 feet into the forest, edge impacts are more than mere esoteric

considerations of interest to the scientific community, these changes have direct

economic implications for both landowners and society. Recent estimates have placed

the annual costs to the U.S. economy from the biological invasion of invasive species at

approximately $21 billion dollars (Fantle-Lepczyk et al. 2022).




                                               6
 Invasive organisms within terrestrial forest environments tend to be early successional

species that respond favorably to site disturbance. Disruption of native plant cover and the

exposure of the forest floor to sunlight provides an opportunity for these organisms to

establish satellite populations. These populations eventually radiate out into the adjacent

forest, displacing native species and retarding desirable tree regeneration (Bennet et al.

2011). Dispersal (vectoring) mechanisms and/or corridors are required for these

non-native species to colonize new locations and the right-of-way corridors associated

with natural gas pipelines are ideally configured to serve this function.



For years into the future after decommissioning, the landscape legacy of forest

edge from pipeline corridors, access roads and other infrastructure will continue to disrupt

ecosystem functioning as non-native organisms repeatedly colonize exposed areas and

impede desirable tree regeneration.



Invasive species suppression and the eventual restoration of these disturbed sites to

forested systems will require resources of a significant financial and temporal scale. While

published information is scarce, it is in the professional experience of restoration

practitioners in this region that the reasonable reconstruction of forest canopy and

understory diversity can cost between $5,700 and $14,200 per acre. The suppression of

invasive plant species is also a major, recurring expense with the initial years’ treatment

often incurring costs between $1,400 and $3,500 per acre. Invasive treatment in

subsequent years typically drops in cost by approximately 50% per year over the first three

years.



As the effects of forest fragmentation may not immediately manifest themselves following

the disturbance, monitoring is often suggested as a methodology to balance and modify

 the level of fragmenting activity in accordance with the conservation of forest-related

ecosystem services. Unfortunately, these effects may not be linear in nature and thus are

not always amendable to an adaptive management approach. Biological systems may

possess thresholds that provide little indication of impending adverse impacts until

sudden system collapse. It is from within this conceptual framework that a review of the

Constitution Pipeline EA and supporting submissions were undertaken and the following

concerns identified.

VEGETATION



Section 5 - Scope of Environmental Assessment



FERC fails to carry forward the vegetation resource for analysis in the Environmental

Assessment. Twelve years have transpired since the Final Environmental Impact Statement

was published in 2014, and it is unreasonable to assume that substantial changes have not

occurred in the vegetative communities located within the impact area of the Constitution

Pipeline. As an example, in the Environmental Assessment FERC indicates that the

Pennsylvania section of the project was clearcut over a decade ago by Constitution

contractors and then subsequently abandoned without restoration or active management.

The Pennsylvania section represents over one fifth of the project length. As a result of

clearcutting and subsequent abandonment, this vegetative community has absolutely

undergone significant modification.




                                              8
 FERC assumes that the cleared areas have begun to regenerate and that invasive plant

species “may have” colonized these areas. FERC also indicates in the Environmental

Information Request No. 2 (June 25th, 2026), that Constitution has committed to updating

the invasive species surveys following reinstatement of the Certificate Order. This is

circular reasoning as a determination that the vegetation has not undergone “substantial

changes” can only be made after a survey. Undertaking a new survey of this area

would help inform planning and mitigation strategies in a new Environmental Impact

Statement as it serves as a test case for the vegetation changes that can be anticipated

should the project be constructed.



The successional trajectory of the forest systems that have been clearcut and then

abandoned for over a decade will display a species composition and habitat type radically

different from the previous cover type. The introduction and colonization of invasive

species into a disturbed linear corridor of over 25 miles that lacks active management will,

in all probability, be significant. Wind, water, human and animal vectoring will have

distributed seed and plant propagules across this area. A newly cleared linear corridor is

extremely attractive to off-road vehicles – a frequent contributor to invasive plant

dispersal and continual site disruption. It will also attract white-tail deer, a known vector for

the distribution of Japanese Stiltgrass. Both tires and hooves easily facilitate seed

dispersal.



Given the clearcutting and the temporal lag between the FEIS and the EA, a new vegetation

analysis must be a component of the Environmental Assessment. FERC failed to conduct

such an analysis, a critical component to have before the Constitution Project moves

forward. Without a proper understanding of current conditions, it is impossible to assess

and disclose project impacts. The premature issuance of a Certificate would thus be

Invasive Species Management Plans



FERC utilizes the state-specific Invasive Species Management Plans (ISMPs) as a

component of the rationale for not carrying forward vegetation in the EA analysis. As such,

it is important to highlight the major deficits in these plans. Given the high degree of

commonality between both the New York and Pennsylvania plans, the concerns detailed

here are applicable to both documents.



The ISMPs stated goal is to goal is to, “…control the invasive species to the extent that

wetlands and uplands are not dominated by the invasive species to the point where the

functions and values of the systems/habitats are adversely compromised”. However, there

are no measurable metrics indicated in the documents that would allow for quantitative

assessment of progress towards that goal. It is common practice in invasive control

contracts for the land management entity to require a certain percentage of invasive cover

reduction be achieved after a given time frame. This provides a clear benchmark whereby

project success can be measured. Constitution’s Plan lacks such a requirement.



While the ISMPs acknowledge the difficulty in achieving eradication of invasive species

due to issues such as seed drift and/or colonization from off-site locations, they fail to

mention two critical vectoring mechanisms that are of extreme importance when dealing

with right-of-way construction and maintenance:



       (1) the latent seed bank residing in the soil



                                              10
        (2) the chronic encouragement of invasive colonization due to the expansion of edge
habitat.



Depending upon the species, invasive seeds and propagules can survive in the soil for

years. Japanese stiltgrass (Microstegium vimineum) and Autumn Olive (Elaeagnus

umbellate) have both been frequently found within the proposed project ROW.

These species have a seed viability in the soil (the timeframe in which they can lay

dormant) that exceeds five years. This latent seed bank germination cannot be addressed

within the brief three-year time frame in which Constitution intends for treatment and

monitoring.



Constitution recognizes in the Preliminary Migratory Bird and Upland Forest Plan that in the

construction of the project, a significant amount of interior forest will be converted to edge

forest. The nature of edge habitat – disturbed areas of high light penetration, creates ideal

conditions for biological invasion. One of the primary transport mechanisms for invasive

plants are birds that preferentially roost at the forest edge and subsequently defecate

invasive seeds into the understory. It is important to recognize that, until such time that

the forest canopy closes over the right-of-way, the edge habitat that has been created will

be highly susceptible to invasive colonization. Once established, small populations can

expand into off-right-of-way properties and disrupt forest regeneration, soil chemistry,

habitat, hydrology, and ultimately land value. Recognizing the chronic nature of the

biological invasion threat that is promoted by the creation and perpetuation of edge

habitat, it is obvious that a treatment timeframe that only lasts for three years is wholly

inadequate. Invasive suppression needs to continue for the project lifespan as the

perpetuation of edge habitat via the three-year mowing and suppression of tree canopy in

the ROW will create ideal conditions for repeated infestation.

 The ISMPs clearly state that Constitution “will not” treat areas outside its proposed

construction right-of-way for invasive species. This is highly problematic given that the

edge habitat created by the Constitution project will encourage biological invasion in the

adjacent forest lands for the entire service life of the right-of-way. Suppression costs will

eventually fall upon the adjacent property owner should an infestation become

established. As invasive plants can directly impact native tree regeneration, landowners

who are managing their forests for sustainable timber production and/or wildlife will suffer

associated with the creation of forest edge, these funds will be directed towards third

parties, not to the adjacent landowner. In effect, the neighboring property owner will bear

the full costs for managing invasive plant infestations, infestations that are a direct result of

the existence of the ROW.

 CONCLUSION



The current Environmental Assessment for the Constitution Pipeline project is flawed as it

fails to analyze vegetation resources that have, in all probability, substantially changed in

twelve years since the Final Environmental Impact Statement was produced. In

addition, the EA relies upon inadequate Invasive Species Management Plans as part of the

rationale for avoiding updating the vegetation analysis.



Without an updated invasive plant survey and vegetation analysis, mitigation and

management strategies cannot be effectively developed and implemented. Should the

Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity be issued by FERC without a proper

analysis widespread disruption of forest ecosystems and local watershed resources will

occur. Restoration of these systems following the eventual cessation of natural gas

transmission will be a monumental cost incurred by both the taxpaying public and adjacent

private property owners.
